column1: # AI contextual English corrections based on the frozen dictionary record; not human sign-off.

column2: The dictionary records an earlier sense of something mysterious and beyond ordinary understanding.
Keeping one's hands inside one's sleeves while watching from the side.
The original sense was simply doing whatever one wanted; wei means to do.
Announcing commands and issuing orders.
The pointed tip of an awl sticks out through the cloth bag containing it.
Falling down from the sky; jiang means to descend.
Writing a long or elaborate essay on a small topic.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of solemn, respectful caution.
Having no route left to take and no place to turn to.
Bringing a dying person back to life; the expression also praises remarkable medical skill.
Fighting side by side in close coordination.
Not knowing or noticing that something is happening.
Originally, a change in a person's appearance.
Giving no help or benefit to the matter at hand; ji means to help.
Words as sweet as honey.
The dictionary links bright skies and the life-giving sun with an earlier sense of a peaceful, prosperous age.
Running far away like a wild animal or flying far away like a bird.
Originally, occupying a high position.
Having no way out and facing a fatal dead end.
An unknown low-ranking soldier; zu is an old word for a soldier.
Gui and ju are tools for drawing circles and right angles; the image refers to following established standards.
Being unable to move forward or retreat without difficulty.
A boat travels with its sail full and the wind behind it.
Taking another person's place or position.
Smoke and clouds disperse and disappear.
Originally, going into battle alone, without support.
Something is as easy as turning over one's palm.
In the Daoist image recorded by the dictionary, spiritual attainment transforms an ordinary body into an immortal one.
Going about alone and not joining other people.
Yi means unusual. The dictionary uses tian kai to explain fanciful imagining; it does not provide a separate historical literal meaning.
One year follows another.
Being so powerful that every battle can be won.
Flowers bloom attractively but produce no fruit.
The earlier expression describes disregarding both the law and moral order.
Several things merge into a single whole.
Chun chun describes the restless wriggling of small crawling creatures.
The pointed ends of two needles face each other.
A pass or checkpoint; the whole expression identifies a decisive juncture.
Feeling heavy-headed, exhausted, and ready to fall asleep.
The image compares people's suffering to ever-deeper water and ever-hotter fire.
Originally, forming a single united whole.
A fish finds the water it needs.
Running along a road in the opposite direction.
Leaving events to fate instead of making one's own effort to change them.
The dictionary records an earlier interpretation of passing from birth to death; the current idiom emphasizes mortal danger.
Jing is a small path and ting a courtyard; the dictionary explains the combined expression as a great separation or disparity.
Pouring oil onto a fire.
Cutting something into two pieces with one stroke of a blade.
Opponents collapse or flee wherever a force advances.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of mechanically borrowing words and phrases from another person's writing.
Empty hands, without a weapon or any equipment.
The dictionary notes a Daoist connection between being and non-being, then explains the phrase as claiming that something exists when it does not.
Struggling in the moments before death in an attempt to prolong life.
Geng sheng means renewed life or recovery. The whole expression emphasizes rebuilding through one's own effort.
A disorderly group resembles a flock of crows gathered together temporarily.
The dictionary records an earlier reference to a serious classic conforming to moral standards.
Xing originally refers to interest or enthusiasm, and cai to spirit or expression; the whole phrase describes high spirits and exuberance.
Placing one's feet firmly on solid ground.
Throwing stones at someone who has fallen into a well instead of helping them.
Barely prolonging the final breaths of a dying person.
Sleeping with one's pillow raised, free from worries.
Covering other people's eyes and ears so that they cannot see or hear.
A skilled butcher's blade moves freely through the spaces between joints.
Originally, applying light colors with gentle strokes in a painting.
Before painting bamboo, the painter already holds its complete form in mind.
The dictionary records a Buddhist sense referring to a person's original nature.
No sound, movement, or sign of activity; xi refers to breath or a trace of activity.
Cha here means rather or somewhat, and qiang means to hearten or inspire. The older wording expresses giving some encouragement; the modern idiom means reasonably satisfactory.
Blowing one's own trumpet and beating one's own drum.
A crane stands among a flock of chickens.
Originally, strategically useful terrain on which military force could be employed.
Driving out and exterminating completely.
The familiar things an old scholar repeatedly says.
Links are joined one after another like the links of a chain.
Dark smoke and unhealthy mountain vapors. The dictionary records the old belief that such vapors caused disease.
Not mentioning even a single word about something.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of sincerity and openness to learning; the present expression describes complete emptiness.
Removing weeds together with their roots so that they cannot grow again.
A very large and cumbersome object.
Clouds and smoke drift past one's eyes.
A living hell in the human world.
A thousand articles all follow the same formula.
Holding an army in place without allowing it to move into action.
Removing three sides of a bird-catching net and leaving only one side in place.
A bird astonishes everyone with a single call.
People with the same illness sympathize with each other.
Not being worth even one small coin.
Tong yang refers to pain and itching, figuratively to something important. The whole expression says that the matter has no important effect.
The dictionary records an earlier use for beautiful, profound writing that deeply shakes the reader's emotions.
In the traditional image, immortals or Daoist adepts summon wind and rain by magical power.
Originally, becoming famous after success in the imperial examinations.
Using one's strength to turn back a huge, violent wave.
Turning danger into safety; yi originally evokes level, easy ground.
Crossing a river together in the same boat.
The recorded image is of eating sugar cane from its top toward its sweeter lower end, so that each mouthful improves.
A check that cannot be cashed because the promised funds are unavailable.
A silkworm spins a cocoon and encloses itself inside it.
The dictionary records an earlier description of the intricate, interlocking structure of a palace.
No one asks where the ferry crossing is.
Not blaming someone for something that has already happened or been done.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of substantial, sincere, and solemn behavior.
Floating with the waves and being carried along by the current.
Horses harnessed side by side run at the same speed.
An entire army is destroyed.
Hands and feet are parts of the same body; here they stand for siblings and a very close bond.
Seeing the sky and sun again after being shut away.
A human life is involved; guan tian emphasizes that the matter is of the utmost importance.
Originally, dishonest producers cut labor or materials to increase profit at the expense of quality.
The dictionary associates the expression with Jiang Yan, whose later writing was said to lack the brilliance of his youth.
Floodwater rises above a person's head and threatens to drown them.
A mythical heavenly horse gallops through the air.
The recorded image is of fighting cocks sharpening their beaks before another round of combat.
Both hands, both knees, and the head touch the ground in a deeply respectful Buddhist bow.
A fierce animal bares its teeth and brandishes its claws.
The traditional story pairs a wolf with an imagined companion called a bei, using their different legs to help each other harm livestock.
Originally, one's claims exceeded one's actual abilities.
Emerging from a thatched cottage; the recorded story connects this image with Zhuge Liang beginning his public career.
Originally, each person receives what satisfies them or suits their needs.
Pushing the waves and making them grow larger.
Moving from a dark, narrow place into a broad and bright one.
Strong wind and heavy rain.
Originally, frightening and malevolent spirits.
Demons, monsters, and ghosts.
Riding on a tiger's back and being unable to get off safely.
The image is of placing three seals over one's mouth to prevent careless speech.
Far beyond the highest clouds and heavens.
Throwing something into an eastward-flowing river and letting it be carried away.
Thousands of fine threads, too numerous to count.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of expansive or elaborate speech; the common current sense criticizes arrogant, irresponsible remarks.
Mao Sui volunteers and recommends himself for a task in the recorded historical story.
Wei functions like is, and gu suggests a difficult predicament. Moving forward or backward both lead to difficulty.
Bending the thumb first when counting on one's fingers, indicating first place.
Standing high and looking far into the distance.
A tiny spark of fire.
Originally, riding ahead of the others in a cavalry charge.
Sweeping everything away in one motion.
Bian fu refers to the edges of cloth and, by extension, neat dress and appearance. The whole expression describes neglecting such neatness.
Finding it difficult to take even a single step.
Trying to catch fish in muddy water, where confusion makes concealment easier.
A remarkably effective medicine, imagined as capable of bringing the dying back to life.
Being afraid of both what lies ahead and what lies behind.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of rulers and ministers pooling their efforts and ideas.
Originally, becoming exhausted by constantly traveling on official orders.
Climbing over mountains and crossing ridges; the expression evokes the difficulty of a long journey on foot.
Holding a game piece and being unable to decide where to place it.
The Buddhist image refers to good fortune across a previous life, the present life, and a future life.
Originally, having large hands and feet.
Nets spread through the sky and over the ground, forming an enclosure in every direction.
The mountains and waterways have come to an end, leaving no route onward.
The dictionary records an earlier sense of refraining from causing disturbances so that ordinary people can live peacefully.
Offering one's sincere heart to another person, as an image of complete trust and openness.
Yang means illness. The older expression describes being safe and free of illness.
Originally, laying down laws and agreeing with the people that they would be observed; later, agreeing on a few simple rules.
